claim: p53 null HAP-1 cells exhibit a doubling of stalled replication forks compared to wild-type p53 HAP-1 cells (35% vs 18%).
source: We find a doubling of stalled forks in CRISPR/CAS9- engineered p53- null human HAP-1 cells compared to cells with wild-type (WT) p53 (Figure 1B; 35% stalled forks in p53 null 18% WT p53 HAP-1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data from DNA fiber spreading assays shown in Figure 1B, with specific percentages provided.

claim: p53 deficiency results in decreased new origin firing during replication stress.
source: Unexpectedly, we find that increased fork stalling in p53 null cells is accompanied by a decrease, rather than an increase, in new origin firing compared to both WT p53 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; 20% newly fired origins in HAP-1 cells, respectively, and 9% newly fired origins in HAP-1 p53 null cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, showing quantitative measurements of new origin firing.

claim: GOF p53 R172H mutant MEFs show increased stalled replication forks (36%) compared to WT p53 MEFs (15%).
source: These cells show both an increase in stalled replication forks, and fewer newly fired forks compared to WT p53 MEFs (Figure 1C; 36% stalled forks in p53 R172H MEF and 15% in WT MEF and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber spreading assays in primary MEFs, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: p53 R172P mutant mice exhibit less severe tumor development compared to p53 null mice despite loss of transcriptional activation and apoptosis.
source: Murine p53 R172P corresponds to a rare human polymorphism R175P, which results in loss of transcriptional activation and apoptosis resembling p53 null (Liu et al., 2004). Yet, tumor development is markedly less severe in p53 R172P mice compared to p53 null mice, suggesting alternative mechanisms contribute to tumor progression besides transcriptional regulation of apoptosis with this mutation (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2004, which provides evidence from mouse models.

claim: p53 R172P MEFs show only moderate increase in fork stalling compared to p53 R172H.
source: We therefore tested p53 R172P MEFs and find that they only show a moderate increase in fork stalling compared to p53 R172H (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: p53 S47 is a breast-cancer predisposition polymorphism in African-descent populations.
source: To further examine the possible link of failed p53-mediated replication restart and cancer, we tested p53 S47 (P47S), which is a breast-cancer pre-disposition polymorphism in African-descent populations (Jennis et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jennis et al., 2016.

claim: p53 S47 is largely transcriptionally active including for p21 and remains proficient for apoptosis.
source: It is largely transcriptionally active including for p21 (Felley-Bosco et al., 1993; Jennis et al., 2016); it remains proficient for apoptosis (Felley-Bosco et al., 1993; Jennis et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Felley-Bosco et al., 1993 and Jennis et al., 2016.

claim: p53 S47 mice are tumor prone.
source: Yet, p53 S47 mice are tumor prone, and p53 S47 contributes to breast cancer risk in African populations (Jennis et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jennis et al., 2016 and Murphy et al., 2017.

claim: p53 S47 slows cell growth similar to WT p53, consistent with intact cell-cycle checkpoint functions.
source: We find that S47 slows cell growth similar to WT p53 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) consistent with intact cell-cycle check-point functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MTT proliferation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: p53 S47 primary MEFs exhibit loss-of-function for replication restart with 31% stalled forks versus 15% in WT MEF.
source: Furthermore, we find that p53 S47 primary MEFs exhibit a loss-of-function (LOF) for replication restart, as measured by an increase in stalled forks upon HU treatment compared to WT MEF cultures (Figure 1D; 31% stalled forks in p53 S47 MEF versus 15% in WT MEF).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: p53 S47 MEFs resemble p53 null MEFs in their inability to restart forks (31% vs 34% stalled forks).
source: Moreover, p53 S47 MEFs resemble p53 null MEFs in their inability to restart forks (Figure 1D; 34% stalled forks in p53 null MEF).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both p53 null MEF and p53 S47 MEFs show defects in new fork initiation (9% and 8% vs 21% in WT).
source: Similar to p53 null HAP-1 and GOF R172H MEF cells, both p53 null MEF and p53 S47 MEFs show defects in new fork initiation (Figure 1E; 21% newly fired origins in p53 WT MEF versus 9% and 8% in p53 S47 MEF and p53 null MEF).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Human p53 S47-expressing H1299 cells show increased stalled forks (38%) compared to WT p53-expressing H1299 cells (13%).
source: We found an increase in stalled forks that resembles p53-null H1299 cells. Both p53 null and p53 S47 H1299 cells exhibit a substantial increase in stalled forks compared to WT p53-expressing H1299 cells (Figure 1F; 13% stalled forks in p53 WT, 38% in p53 S47, and 45% in null H1299 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DNA fiber assays in H1299 cells shown in Figure 1F.

claim: p53 promoted replication restart can be genetically separated from its transcription-activation function in cell cycle progression and apoptosis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that p53 promoted replication restart can be genetically separated from its transcription-activation function in cell cycle progression and apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing p53 S47 retains transcription and apoptosis functions but loses replication restart function.

claim: Restart defects cause cellular sensitivity to replication stalling agents, as seen for cells with BLM defects.
source: Restart defects cause cellular sensitivity to replication stalling agents, as seen for cells with BLM defects (Davies et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2004.

claim: p53 S47-expressing H1299 cells are sensitive to replication stalling agents HU and mitomycin C.
source: We find that p53 S47-expressing H1299 cells are sensitive to replication stalling agents HU (Figure 2A) and mitomycin C (MMC; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell survival assays shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The cellular replication stress phenotype is masked when p53 mutations additionally inactivate apoptosis and cell-cycle checkpoint functions.
source: This cellular replication stress phenotype is masked when the p53 mutations additionally inactivate apoptosis and cell-cycle check-point functions, such as in p53 null H1299 cells (Figure 2A and B) or p53 null compared to WT mammary epithelial MCF10A cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell survival assays shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: p53 functions in replication restart suppress cellular sensitivity to replication stress.
source: Collectively, the data with apoptosis-proficient p53 S47 implies that p53 functions in replication restart suppresses cellular sensitivity to replication stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing p53 S47 cells are sensitive to replication stress despite intact apoptosis.

claim: Primary MEF p53 R172P exhibited less micronuclei with replication stalling (8%) compared to p53 R172H (26%).
source: Consistent with an intermediate phenotype for replication restart, primary MEF p53 R172P exhibited less micronuclei with replication stalling compared to p53 R172H (Figure 2D; average of 8% micronuclei in p53 R172P and 26% in p53 R172H) albeit considerably more than WT p53 MEFs (none detected in WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from micronuclei assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Human p53 S47-expressing cells showed a marked increase in cells containing micronuclei (20%) compared to WT p53-expressing H1299 cells (5%).
source: With replication stalling, human p53 S47-expressing cells showed a marked increase in cells containing micronuclei compared to WT p53-expressing H1299 cells (Figure 2E average of 20% in p53 S47% and 5% in p53 WT H1299 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from micronuclei assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Micronuclei instability in p53 null H1299 cells is significantly higher (12%) than in WT p53 H1299 cells (5%).
source: Micronuclei instability in p53 null H1299 cells similarly is significantly higher than in WT p53 H1299 cells (Figure 2E; average of 12%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from micronuclei assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The genomic instability data corresponds with restart defects rather than transcription functions found in the respective p53 mutants.
source: Taken together, the genomic instability data corresponds with restart defects rather than transcription functions found in the respective p53 mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing genomic instability phenotypes across different p53 mutants with varying transcription and restart functions.

claim: p53 functions are required for resolving replication stress-dependent genome instability and can contribute to tumor suppression.
source: The data suggest that p53 functions are required for resolving replication stress-dependent genome instability and by implication can contribute to tumor suppression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing p53 defects lead to genomic instability.

claim: p53 associates with nascent-labeled DNA in HEK293 cells.
source: We found that p53 associates with nascent-labeled DNA in HEK293 cells (Figure 3A, IP fraction, E, 3.8 normalized to chromatin protein ORC2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from iPOND assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p53 association with nascent DNA is reduced with a thymidine chase, suggesting p53 travels with the active replication fork.
source: Similarly, we find that the p53 association with nascent DNA is reduced with a thymidine chase, suggesting p53 travels with the active replication fork (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from iPOND assays shown in Figure 3A and inference about p53 behavior.

claim: Replication stalling by HU retains p53, but not PCNA at stalled forks.
source: Replication stalling by HU retains p53, but not PCNA at stalled forks (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from iPOND assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p53 has a direct role at active and stalled DNA replication forks.
source: Taken together, the data suggests a direct role for p53 at active and stalled DNA replication forks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the iPOND experimental data showing p53 association with replication forks.

claim: MLL3 association with replication forks in unperturbed cells is similar in p53 null (12 sites/cell) and WT HAP-1 cells (11 sites/cell).
source: MLL3 association with replication forks in unperturbed cells is similar in p53 null and WT HAP-1 cells (Figure 3C; 11 MLL3-bound replication sites per cell in WT p53 and 12 sites in p53 null HAP-1 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Upon replication stalling with HU, there is a marked increase in MLL3-bound replication sites in WT (17 sites) but not in p53 null HAP-1 cells (13 sites).
source: Upon replication stalling with HU, we see a marked increase in MLL3-bound replication sites in WT, but not in p53 null human HAP-1 cells (Figure 3D; 17 MLL3-bound sites in WT and 13 in p53 null HAP-1 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The data suggest inefficient MLL3 recruitment to forks upon replication stalling in the absence of p53.
source: These data suggest inefficient MLL3 recruitment to forks upon replication stalling in the absence of p53.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the SIRF experimental data showing reduced MLL3 recruitment in p53 null cells.

claim: MLL3-mediated chromatin opening is implicated in MRE11 nuclease recruitment to stalled replication forks.
source: MLL3-mediated chromatin opening is implicated in MRE11 nuclease recruitment to stalled replication forks (Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016), a repair nuclease that is needed for efficient replication restart (Trenz et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016 and Trenz et al., 2006.

claim: There is increased MRE11-bound replication sites in WT (30 sites) but not in p53 null HAP-1 cells (18 sites) when challenged with HU.
source: Consistently, we find increased MRE11-bound replication sites in WT, but not in p53 null HAP-1 cells when challenged with HU (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 30 MRE11-bound replication sites/cell in WT and 18 in p53 null HAP-1 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: p53 promotes local chromatin responses that aid MRE11 recruitment to stalled forks, as necessary for replication restart.
source: Collectively, these data suggest a mechanism whereby p53 promotes local chromatin responses that aid MRE11 recruitment to stalled forks, as necessary for replication restart (Trenz et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citation to Trenz et al., 2006.

claim: p53 is implicated in suppressing excessive repair by homologous recombination (HR) to balance genomic stability.
source: p53 is implicated in suppressing excessive repair by homologous recombination (HR) to balance genomic stability (Bertrand et al., 2004; Saintigny et al., 1999; Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2004, Saintigny et al., 1999, and Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: In p53 null HAP-1 cells, there is less RAD51 at local stalled replication forks (19 sites) compared to WT p53 (24 sites).
source: Instead, in p53 null HAP-1 cells, we find less RAD51 at local stalled replication forks (Figure 4A; 24 RAD51-bound replication sites/cell in WT p53 and 19 in p53 null HAP-1 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HCT116 cells expressing GOF p53 R248W show increased RAD51 fork-localization compared to WT-expressing HCT116.
source: In contrast, HCT116 cells expressing GOF p53 R248W show increased RAD51 fork-localization compared to WT-expressing HCT116, as do LOF mutant p53 S47-expressing H1299 cells compared to cells with WT p53 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: p53 null Saos-2 show an increase in RAD51 SIRF signals, which is repressed with expression of mutant p53 GOF R175H and R273H.
source: p53 null Saos-2 show an increase in RAD51 SIRF signals, which is repressed with expression of mutant p53 GOF R175H and R273H.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays in Saos-2 cells.

claim: The results do not support a correlation between RAD51 recruitment to forks and fork instability in these cells.
source: Together, these results do not support a correlation between RAD51 recruitment to forks and fork instability in these cells, but instead suggest alternative causation for the observed genomic instability in p53 mutant cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing variable RAD51 recruitment patterns across different p53 mutants.

claim: Spontaneous SCE is independent of RAD51 and BRCA2 but involves the single-strand annealing (SSA) protein RAD52.
source: Reports increasingly suggest that spontaneous SCE is independent of RAD51 and BRCA2 (Bai and Symington, 1996; Clémence Claussin et al., 2017; Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016), but instead involves the single-strand annealing (SSA) protein RAD52 (Thorpe et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Bai and Symington, 1996; Clémence Claussin et al., 2017; Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016; and Thorpe et al., 2006.

claim: There is a marked increase of RAD52 bound to stalled forks in p53-null cells (MFI of 762) compared to WT (MFI of 494).
source: Using SIRF analysis, we find a marked increase of RAD52 bound to stalled forks in p53-null cells (Figure 4C). As the signals were too abundant to be individually counted, we used the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) as a quantitative readout (Figure 4C, MFI of 494 in p53 null and 762 in p53 WT HAP-1 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 4C using mean fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: RAD52 recruitment is stronger at low compared to high concentration of HU.
source: Notably, we see stronger RAD52 recruitment at low compared to high concentration of HU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RAD52 recruitment to stalled forks is stronger than to bona fide DNA breaks.
source: The former condition is less favorable for DSB formation, suggesting RAD52 recruitment to stalled forks is stronger than to bona fide DNA breaks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observation that RAD52 recruitment is higher at low HU concentrations.

claim: There is an increase in RAD52 recruitment in all p53-defective cell lines tested irrespective of the nature of the p53 defect.
source: Strikingly, we find an increase in RAD52 recruitment in all p53-defective cell lines tested irrespective of the nature of the p53 defect. This includes HCT116 GOF p53 R248W (Figure 4D), Saos-2 p53 null, Saos-2 GOF p53 R175H, Saos-2 GOF p53 R273H, and H1299 LOF p53 S47 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E) compared to respective WT p53-expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The increased RAD52 recruitment to stalled forks was not caused by transcriptional deregulations in p53-defective cells, as RAD52 protein levels remained unchanged.
source: This pathway imbalance was not caused by transcriptional deregulations in p53-defective cells, as RAD52 protein levels remained unchanged with or without p53, further supporting a transcription-independent function of p53 at stalled forks (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Western blots shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The observed increased RAD52 recruitment to stalled forks is likely a consequence of defective replication restart.
source: Thus, the observed increased RAD52 recruitment to stalled forks is likely a consequence of defective replication restart.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing RAD52 recruitment increases in p53-defective cells with restart defects.

claim: POLθ is implicated in promoting error-prone MMEJ at replication-associated DNA ends.
source: POLθ is implicated in promoting error-prone MMEJ at replication-associated DNA ends (Roerink et al., 2014), which includes collapsed or reversed replication forks.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Roerink et al., 2014.

claim: There is an increase of mutant p53 S47 association with POLθ in unchallenged H1299 cells (24 associations/cell), which is further enhanced with replication stalling (38 associations/cell).
source: We find an increase of mutant p53 S47 association with POLθ in unchallenged H1299 cells, which is further enhanced with replication stalling (Figure 5A, 24 associations per cell without and 38 with HU).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PLA assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT p53-POLθ associations remain limited even with replication stalling (6 associations without HU and 15 with HU).
source: Notably, WT p53-POLθ associations remain limited even with replication stalling (Figure 5A, average of 6 associations without and 15 with HU), suggesting pathway tipping toward mutagenic MMEJ in p53-defective cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PLA assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Inhibition of MRE11 by PFM39 greatly increased WT p53-POLθ association with replication stalling (from 15 to 50/cell average).
source: Inhibition of MRE11 by PFM39 greatly increased WT p53-POLθ association with replication stalling (Figure 5A, an increase from 15 to 50/cell average with PFM39).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PLA assays with MRE11 inhibitor shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MRE11 inactivation can partially pheno-copy p53 deficiency at replication forks.
source: This observation suggests that MRE11 inactivation can partially pheno-copy p53 deficiency at replication forks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing MRE11 inhibition increases POLθ association similar to p53 defects.

claim: POLθ interactions with RAD52 increased in GOF p53 R248W HCT116 cells.
source: Of note, we find POLθ interactions with RAD52 increased in GOF p53 R248W HCT116 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), giving rise to the possibility that POLθ may collaborate with RAD52 in p53-defective cells rather than acting in separate pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PLA assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is increased POLθ recruitment to stalled forks in p53-null HAP-1 cells.
source: Consistently, we find increased POLθ recruitment to stalled forks in p53-null HAP-1 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inactivation of MRE11 nuclease in WT HAP-1 cells causes a significantly increase in recruitment of POLθ to stalled forks.
source: Similarly, inactivation of MRE11 nuclease in WT HAP-1 cells causes a significantly increase in recruitment of POLθ to stalled forks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays with MRE11 inhibition.

claim: The data uncover p53-MRE11 repression of mutagenic RAD52 and POLθ processes at replication forks.
source: Together these data uncover p53-MRE11 repression of mutagenic RAD52 and POLθ processes at replication forks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing increased RAD52 and POLθ activity when p53 or MRE11 are defective.

claim: SSA predominantly results in larger deletion mutations, while MMEJ is signified by microhomology at repair junctions along with deletions.
source: RAD52/SSA and POLθ/MMEJ pathways allow the prediction of specific mutation signatures; SSA predominantly results in larger deletion mutations, while MMEJ is signified by microhomology at repair junctions along with deletions (Jasin and Rothstein, 2013; Wood and Doublié, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jasin and Rothstein, 2013 and Wood and Doublié, 2016.

claim: Seven mutational signatures are increased in p53-defective breast cancers.
source: Seven mutational signatures are increased in p53-defective breast cancers (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Of the seven signatures, only signatures 3 and signature 5 are significantly increased in p53 defective compared to WT p53 breast cancers.
source: However, of these seven signatures, only signatures 3 and signature 5 are significantly increased in p53 defective compared to WT p53 breast cancers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B);
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: COSMIC signature 3 is defined by larger deletion mutations (>3 bp) with microhomology at break junctions, consistent with expected RAD52 and POLθ mutation spectra.
source: COSMIC signature 3 is defined by larger deletion mutations (>3 bp) with microhomology at break junctions, consistent with expected RAD52 and POLθ mutation spectra.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of COSMIC signature definitions and inference connecting it to RAD52/POLθ pathways.

claim: COSMIC signature 5 shows T > C transition mutations at ApTpN context with thus far unknown etiology.
source: COSMIC signature 5 shows T > C transition mutations at ApTpN context with thus far unknown etiology.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of COSMIC signature definitions.

claim: POLθ has a stark preference for T > C transition mutations (error-rate of 42 × 10−4, 4–40 fold higher than any other possible mutation rate) as seen within a known CATCC hotspot.
source: POLθ was reported to have a stark preference for T > C transition mutations (error-rate of 42 × 10−4, 4–40 fold higher than any other possible mutation rate) as seen within a known CATCC hotspot (Arana et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arana et al., 2008.

claim: POLθ may contribute to COSMIC signature 5 etiology.
source: Thus, our combined data uncovers the possibility of POLθ mediated origin of COSMIC signature 5.
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting POLθ mutation preferences with COSMIC signature 5 characteristics.

claim: COSMIC signatures are in agreement with increased RAD52 and POLθ pathway usage in p53 mutant breast cancers.
source: Collectively, we find COSMIC signatures are in agreement with increased RAD52 and POLθ pathway usage in p53 mutant breast cancers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational analysis of TCGA data and experimental findings.

claim: 2/3 of all mutations found across cancers are caused by errors occurring during proliferation.
source: As previously hypothesized (Cox et al., 2000), recent findings formalized that 2/3 of all mutations found across cancers are caused by errors occurring during proliferation (Tomasetti et al., 2017), highlighting the critical importance of protective mechanisms during DNA replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2000 and Tomasetti et al., 2017.

claim: Early studies found p53 is activated at stalled replication forks.
source: Intriguingly, early studies found p53 is activated at stalled replication forks (Gottifredi et al., 2001; Kumari et al., 2004), which are a source for genomic instability requiring distinct replication fork stability pathways (Branzei and Foiani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gottifredi et al., 2001 and Kumari et al., 2004.

claim: p53 interacts with BLM helicase at replication forks and represses HR in S-phase upon DNA damage, independent of its G1-S and transactivation activity.
source: p53 interacts with BLM helicase at replication forks and represses HR in S-phase upon DNA damage, independent of its G1-S and transactivation activity (Bertrand et al., 2004; Janz and Wiesmüller, 2002; Saintigny and Lopez, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2004, Janz and Wiesmüller, 2002, and Saintigny and Lopez, 2002.

claim: p53 was found to interact with DNA POLι.
source: Hinting at a direct p53 replication function, recently p53 was found to interact with DNA POLι (Hampp et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hampp et al., 2016.

claim: p53 deletion in U2OS cells was reported to slow unperturbed replication.
source: Moreover, p53 deletion in U2OS cells was reported to slow unperturbed replication (Klusmann et al., 2016), although this was suggested to require p53 transcription function, while p53 functions in DNA damage response are not.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klusmann et al., 2016.

claim: p53 suppresses replication genomic instability independent of transcription activation.
source: By delineating human and murine separation-of-function p53 alleles, we find that p53 null and gain-of-function (GOF) mutations exhibit defects in restart of stalled or damaged DNA replication forks that drive genomic instability, which isgenetically separable from transcription activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from separation-of-function p53 mutants.

claim: p53 defects or depletion unexpectedly allow mutagenic RAD52 and POLθ pathways to hijack stalled forks.
source: Importantly, p53 defects or depletion unexpectedly allow mutagenic RAD52 and POLθ pathways to hijack stalled forks, which we find reflected in p53 defective breast-cancer patient COSMIC mutational signatures.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SIRF assays and computational analysis of TCGA data.

claim: p53 is a keystone regulator of replication homeostasis within a DNA restart network.
source: These data uncover p53 as a keystone regulator of replication homeostasis within a DNA restart network.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing p53's role in coordinating multiple restart pathways.

claim: In breast cancers, p53 mutations are associated with more aggressive and triple negative breast cancers.
source: In breast cancers, p53 mutations are associated with more aggressive and triple negative breast cancers (Turner et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2013.

claim: Aggressive breast cancers respond to chemotherapy including platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors initially, but develop resistance thereafter.
source: Similar to high serous ovarian cancers, these aggressive cancers respond to chemotherapy including platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors initially, but develop resistance thereafter (Luvero et al., 2014; Wahba and El-Hadaad, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luvero et al., 2014 and Wahba and El-Hadaad, 2015.

claim: The most consistent defect for both null and GOF p53 mutants in cancers is the loss of p53 transcriptional responses to regulate apoptosis and cell cycle arrest.
source: To date, the most consistent defect for both null and GOF p53 mutants in cancers is the loss of p53 transcriptional responses to regulate apoptosis and cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about p53 function.

claim: Murine p53 R172P retains much of its tumor suppression function despite loss of transcriptional induction and loss of apoptosis.
source: Murine p53 R172P, corresponding to human R175P, retains much of its tumor suppression function despite loss of transcriptional induction and loss of apoptosis (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2004.

claim: p53 mutations in the transactivation domain and p53 acetylation mutations severely inhibit p53 induction of apoptosis and senescence, yet exhibit a mild and delayed tumor onset.
source: Similarly, p53 mutations in the transactivation domain and p53 acetylation mutations severely inhibit p53 induction of apoptosis and senescence, yet exhibit a mild and delayed tumor onset (Li et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2012 and Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: p53 interacts with MLL3/4 histone methyltransferases.
source: p53 also has seemingly disparate cellular functions including during metabolism and epigenetic control, that is through its interaction with MLL3/4 histone methyltransferases (Pfister et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015), although the contribution of these functions to tumor suppression is not fully understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pfister et al., 2015 and Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: ATM mediates p53 phosphorylation as part of a DNA stress response.
source: In response to DNA damage, ATM mediates p53 phosphorylation as part of a DNA stress response (Saito et al., 2002), which is facilitated by PTIP (Jowsey et al., 2004), a BRCT domain containing protein that is part of the MLL3/4 complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2002 and Jowsey et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of p53 does not change DSB repair rates by HR when measured in specific induced break assays.
source: loss of p53 does not change DSB repair rates by HR when measured in specific induced break assays (Willers et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Willers et al., 2001.

claim: p53 has a prominent DNA-binding domain and RPA interaction sites.
source: p53 has a prominent DNA-binding domain and RPA interaction sites (Romanova et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanova et al., 2004.

claim: MLL3 promotes H3K4 histone methylation to mark open chromatin.
source: MLL3 promotes H3K4 histone methylation to mark open chromatin (Ruthenburg et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ruthenburg et al., 2007.

claim: MRE11 impairment promotes progression and invasiveness of mammary hyperplasia in mouse models similar to p53 inactivation.
source: Supporting this concept, MRE11 impairment, which we show phenocopies p53 defects at stalled forks, promotes progression and invasiveness of mammary hyperplasia in mouse models similar to p53 inactivation (Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2013.

claim: p53 is phosphorylated by ATM at S46, which is decreased in p53 S47.
source: p53 is phosphorylated by ATM at S46, which is decreased in p53 S47 (Jennis et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jennis et al., 2016.

claim: At residues D48/D49, p53 can directly interact with single-strand binding protein RPA.
source: Intriguingly, at the adjacent residues D48/D49, p53 can directly interact with single-strand binding protein RPA (Romanova et al., 2004), which is implicated in replication fork remodeling (Neelsen and Lopes, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Romanova et al., 2004 and Neelsen and Lopes, 2015.

claim: RPA interaction mutations deregulate recombination reactions without affecting transactivation reactions.
source: Specifically, RPA interaction mutations deregulate recombination reactions without affecting transactivation reactions (Romanova et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanova et al., 2004.

claim: The latest identified Fanconi Anemia tumor suppressor is the RFWD3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates p53.
source: The latest identified Fanconi Anemia tumor suppressor is the RFWD3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates p53 (Feeney et al., 2017; Inano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feeney et al., 2017 and Inano et al., 2017.

claim: A Fanconi Anemia phenotypes causing patient mutation in RFWD3 leads to deregulation of RPA reactions at the replication fork.
source: Furthermore, a Fanconi Anemia phenotypes causing patient mutation in RFWD3 leads to deregulation of RPA reactions at the replication fork (Inano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Inano et al., 2017.

claim: p53 could feasibly be a vital player in the Fanconi Anemia pathway through its replication function.
source: We therefore propose that p53 could feasibly be a vital player in the Fanconi Anemia pathway through its replication function, and it will be exciting to decipher this relationship.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the connections between p53, RFWD3, and RPA.

claim: MRE11 is a nuclease known to promote restart after replication stalling.
source: We establish here that at forks, p53 controls MRE11, a nuclease known to promote restart after replication stalling (Trenz et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Trenz et al., 2006.

claim: Other prominent p53 collaborating proteins including BLM helicase, ATM, and PARP-1 all promote replication restart.
source: Other prominent p53 collaborating proteins including BLM helicase (Davies et al., 2007), ATM (Trenz et al., 2006), and PARP-1 (Bryant et al., 2009) all promote replication restart.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2007, Trenz et al., 2006, and Bryant et al., 2009.

claim: PARP, BLM helicase and RPA promote and repress replication fork reversal.
source: PARP, BLM helicase and RPA promote and repress replication fork reversal (Neelsen and Lopes, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Neelsen and Lopes, 2015.

claim: Fork reversal is readily observed in cancer cells at low concentrations of replication stalling agents.
source: While it is unclear whether fork reversal is required for normal replication restart, it is readily observed in cancer cells at low concentrations of replication stalling agents (Zellweger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zellweger et al., 2015.

claim: In the absence of fork reversal control and stabilization by p53 regulated players, RAD52/POLθ pathways hijack the free DNA end to invade replication ahead or behind the replication fork as an intramolecular reaction.
source: In the absence of fork reversal control and stabilization by p53 regulated players, our model suggests that RAD52/POLθ pathways hijack the free DNA end to invade replication ahead or behind the replication fork as an intramolecular reaction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data and proposed model.

claim: In mammary tumor suppression, p53 cooperates with BRCA1/2.
source: In mammary tumor suppression, p53 cooperates with BRCA1/2 (Jonkers et al., 2001; Ludwig et al., 1997), which is often associated with more aggressive and resistant tumors, although the mechanism of this collaboration has been elusive.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jonkers et al., 2001 and Ludwig et al., 1997.

claim: Gene internal deletion and/or point mutations within the BRCA2 gene can restore reading frames of BRCA2 mutated stop codons in CAPAN-1 pancreatic and POE ovarian cancer cells.
source: Specifically, gene internal deletion and/or point mutations within the BRCA2 gene can restore reading frames of BRCA2 mutated stop codons in CAPAN-1 pancreatic and POE ovarian cancer cells (Sakai et al., 2009; Sakai et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sakai et al., 2009 and Sakai et al., 2008.

claim: Some of the new BRCA2 peptides conferring resistance have extensive internal deletion mutations.
source: Interestingly, while BRCA2 peptide expression is restored, some of these new BRCA2 peptides conferring resistance have extensive internal deletion mutations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited studies about BRCA2 restoration.

claim: Triple negative breast cancers and serous ovarian cancers, which almost exclusively harbor p53 mutations, are often initially sensitive to therapy such as cis-platin drugs.
source: Triple negative breast cancers as well as serous ovarian cancers, which almost exclusively harbor p53 mutations, are often initially sensitive to therapy such as cis-platin drugs (Luvero et al., 2014; Wahba and El-Hadaad, 2015), which cause replication stalling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luvero et al., 2014 and Wahba and El-Hadaad, 2015.

claim: Inhibition of RAD52/POLθ pathways as adjuvant therapy concomitant with initial conventional therapy could offer an actionable strategy for ameliorating aggressive tumor evolution and secondary mutations leading to resistance in p53-defective tumors.
source: our model suggests that inhibition of RAD52/POLθ pathways as adjuvant therapy concomitant with initial conventional therapy could offer an actionable strategy for ameliorating aggressive tumor evolution and secondary mutations leading to resistance in p53-defective tumors.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings and proposed therapeutic implications.

claim: p53 is a key-protein in error-free replication restart.
source: The finding that p53 is a key-protein in error-free replication restart may explain why p53 mutations are a dominant cause of cancer genome instability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing p53's role in replication restart.

claim: p53 mutations are a dominant cause of cancer genome instability.
source: The finding that p53 is a key-protein in error-free replication restart may explain why p53 mutations are a dominant cause of cancer genome instability.
